launch (welcome modal open): The look of a globe seen from space. It is the only projection here that looks like a sphere.
As we all know, the Earth is a sphere. (Sorry, flat earthers.)
Squashing it onto a flat map is where it gets awkward: shapes, areas, distances and directions can't all survive the trip, so every projection picks what to keep and what to bend.
Each choice has its perks and its little lies. On a Mercator map, Greenland looks as big as Africa, which is about 14 times larger.
This tool lets you see those trade-offs for yourself.
Borders and names are adapted from Natural Earth. They are shown for reference, and some are disputed.
[title] Centred on the Greenwich meridian: the Atlantic-centred convention of most Western atlases, with Europe and West Africa in the middle.
[title] A common convention in Chinese school atlases, centred near 105°E: the world splits along the Atlantic instead of the Pacific.
[title] Centred near 20°E, the middle of the African continent. The natural framing for atlases of Africa, and a reminder that a Europe-centred map is a choice, not a fact of nature.
[title] A common convention in American atlases, centred near 90°W: the Americas face you on the globe, and flat maps split the world through Asia.
[title] Centred near 150°E on the western Pacific: East Asia, Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific islands gathered around one ocean, as in atlases from Australia and East Asia.

[title] South at the top, as on the world map published in 2025 by IBGE, Brazil's national mapping institute, and McArthur's Universal Corrective Map (1979). Nothing on a sphere points up: north at the top is a convention, and this view simply picks the other one.

Area, dramatically, away from the equator: Greenland looks as large as Africa despite being 14 times smaller.
